title: Electronic Pioneer Suzanne Ciani Says "Now I Have an Audience"
summary:
Suzanne Ciani was not only present at the beginning of electronic music, but helped develop the technology that became the basis of an entire global genre. Now 80 years old, she is performing her first ever concert in Scotland this weekend, and then she will play a festival in the desert outside Roswell, New Mexico.

Born in Ohio, Ciani earned a master's degree in composition at UC Berkeley, where she met synthesizer designer Don Buchla. She became one of the first people to master the Buchla modular analog synthesizer. In 1974 she founded Ciani/Musica, where she developed sounds for brands including AT&T, General Electric and Coca-Cola. The soda's "pop & pour" sound logo was her creation, and so was the Columbia Pictures intro score. She has released more than 25 studio and live albums and received five Grammy nominations, all in the new age category.

In recent years, Ciani has had what Billboard calls a late career renaissance, thanks to her live modular synthesizer performances. They have brought her into the dance and electronic festival circuit. This weekend she plays Glasgow's Sonica Festival, a longstanding art and experimental music festival. In early November she will play Atomika, a new science and music festival in the remote desert outside Roswell.

Speaking to Billboard over Zoom from her home in Northern California, Ciani said she is selling her house after 34 years because she wanted a new chapter. "The basis of technology is change," she said. The first music she remembers owning was a stack of classical records her mother brought home, including a Rachmaninoff piano concerto and a Grieg piano concerto. She listened to them morning, noon and night.

Asked what album she would recommend to someone new to electronic music, she chose her own Buchla Concerts 1975. She said it came from a cassette tape of a live concert, and that what interests her most is live performance.

Ciani said that when she began, she thought the whole world was excited about the new instruments, but "ran into a wall" because nobody knew what the machine was. "I had no audience then. Now I have an audience. The kids know what's going on. They have the machines. Nobody had them back then."
why_it_matters: Her story shows how pioneers in new technology may feel alone at first, then see later generations adopt the tools they helped create.
